episode_thesis: Richard Brennan, drawing on Dave Dredge's 'Sharpe world' critique, argues that markets are non-linear (long muted regimes interrupted by explosive moves), so risk is the unforeseen, not historical volatility, and portfolios should be built for convexity: small, linear losses on one side of a barbell and amplified gains on the other, with brakes (stops, small bet sizes) that let a strategy accelerate in favorable regimes. Trend following is presented as convexity for opportunity capture as well as protection (anti-martingale scaling into outliers, wide diversification to find them, 'infinite yield' from one trend paying for many small losses), contrasted with concave mean-reversion and negative-skew strategies (LTCM) and with options-based tail protection. The host Niels adds the horizon-dependence of convexity, a counter on defining risk as permanent loss, the open-equity problem for new investors, and the view that a more divergent world with uncoordinated central banks favors trend.

speakers.name: Richard Brennan
speakers.role: Guest; trend follower, East Coast Capital Management (Australia); self-described 'outlier hunter'
speakers.speaker_note: Referred to as Rich by the host; the ledger gives 'Richard Brennan'. Most of the episode is a prepared monologue inspired by Dave Dredge (tail-protection manager, quoted along with Taleb), whose ideas Rich adopts; claims quoting Dredge or Taleb are Rich's reported adoption of them. Caption quirks: 'sharp' for Sharpe, 'bit sizes' for bet sizes, 'night tram' for anti-martingale joke.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are non-linear: long muted regimes alternate with explosive moves and large drawdowns, so an average-volatility description of risk is poor and risk must be managed by adapting to the current regime.
worldview_premises.support: S&P 500 examples (5-year runs of 25%+, 50% GFC drawdown, 1987, 2002)

worldview_premises.premise: Convexity is positive skew: amplify gains when volatility is favorable and cap losses with risk management; concave strategies (mean reversion, negative skew, pattern recognition) earn many small wins and then take sudden large losses when an unpredicted regime arrives.

Volatility is not all bad: adverse volatility should be limited but beneficial volatility exploited; smoothing funds only limit the adverse side and forgo upside, so the car with brakes beats the car optimised for average speed.

The most material market events arise from uncertainty absent from the historical sample, so using history to set expected returns blindsides investors; models trained on history collapse in unprecedented environments and a surviving backtest does not guarantee future survival.
worldview_premises.support: list of crises (1987, 2002, 2008, Asian crisis, LTCM, COVID)

worldview_premises.premise: Smooth linear equity curves are temporary products of a predictable environment and later become concave; managers who lever up predictable returns blow up at regime shift.

Traditional finance rests on five flawed assumptions: historical risk, normality, persistent correlations, estimable returns, and all volatility being bad; risk is a possibility distribution, not a probability distribution (Taleb).
Long calm periods raise fragility (avalanche, flood, forest-fire analogies), so low volatility is not safe, and VaR misses contagion because markets are connected complex adaptive systems.
The 60/40 portfolio rested on a stock-bond correlation that was zero or negative and turned positive, leaving it with no brakes.
Risk is permanent loss of capital, not volatility; few trend followers ever blow up whereas mean-reversion strategies do, and no validated 20-30 year records exist for other styles.
worldview_premises.support: industry observation of blow-ups; absence of long records

worldview_premises.premise: Positive skew optimises long-term compounded wealth, and concave strategies with rare crippling losses create compounding drag.

Options are the most precise hedge for a traditional portfolio because they can be matched to a specific risk (market, correlation), whereas trend following offers less targeted, premium-free convexity, exposed to sudden short-term shocks and whipsaws.

decision_process.practice: Risk each trade as a very small fraction of closed-trade core capital; let unrealised equity run, so the percentage of portfolio at risk is measured against core capital, not against open equity.
decision_process.why: Protects core capital while allowing a trade to explode in value.

decision_process.practice: Take a small initial position when signals suggest a possible material outlier and add as it succeeds, applying an ensemble of models (anti-martingale); never double after losses (martingale).
decision_process.why: Anti-martingale is convex; martingale gives small gains but catastrophic risk.

decision_process.practice: Cut losses short with stops and small bet size as the ultimate stop; build brakes into the process rather than forecasting risk.
decision_process.why: Stop orders can gap in fast markets, whereas small size always bounds the loss.

decision_process.practice: Adapt risk to the current regime (accelerate in favorable regimes, brake in adverse ones) rather than assuming average volatility.
decision_process.why: Convex process responds dynamically to non-linear markets.

decision_process.practice: Trade a very wide range of markets, including unusual commodities, to find outliers wherever they appear.
decision_process.why: The location of the next outlier cannot be forecast.

decision_process.practice: Ride winners until trends exhaust; one outlier (cocoa, an equity rally) pays for dozens of small losses; aim at 'infinite yield'.
decision_process.why: Open-ended payoff pays for the accumulated costs of small controlled losses.

decision_process.practice: Judge trend following on thousands of trades (the last 2,000 or 4,000), not on individual outcomes.
For new capital, allocate AUM based on closed equity so that unrealised equity stays with existing investors; this is a business-of-trend-following adjustment rather than the philosophy itself.
decision_process.why: A new investor entering when open equity is large would face a drawdown that long-standing investors do not.

speakers.evidence_style: First principles, analogies (F1 car, avalanche, flood, forest fire, surfer, pilot, chef, casino martingale) and authority (Dredge, Taleb); little data; cites the existence of long trend-following records and the absence of comparable validated 20-30 year records for other styles as evidence of survival.

current_views.view: January 2025: his firm had a good month driven by commodities like coffee while the SG Trend Index fell, showing dispersion that comes from differing commodity exposure and model design.
current_views.reasoning: Different trend followers hold different exposures and models.

current_views.view: Markets are non-linear and risk comes from the unforeseen; convexity matters most now.
current_views.reasoning: Long muted regimes followed by explosive moves; 60/40 correlation shift.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host, Top Traders Unplugged; veteran hedge fund manager (Dunn Capital)
speakers.speaker_note: Host; the ledger labels him 'host, Dunn Capital'. He states several own views and counter-points, so he is mapped. Claim C14-1 carries a correction: he only raised the new-investor open-equity risk; the closed-equity suggestion is Rich's reply (C14-X1).

worldview_premises.premise: Divergent central bank policy (BOJ hiking, ECB cutting, Fed on hold) creates market divergence and manager dispersion that could suit trend models; a more divergent, less coordinated world favors trend.
Short-term models react to noise (the Nvidia drop of about $600bn reversed within days) that longer-term models ignore.

Convexity depends on horizon: short-term managers and tail funds claim more of it, trend followers' skew has reportedly declined, and longer-term managers can argue that providing convexity daily costs too much bleed and does not matter for long-run results.

A multi-asset portfolio with trend following cushions events nobody imagined; the question is what you are doing about what you are not worried about, and investors who think they are diversified often hold hidden short-volatility exposure.

Risk defined only as permanent loss of capital is too narrow, because complete loss is rare in any strategy and volatility can still feel like risk; long drawdowns hurt investor psychology more than deep short ones (Asness).
The range and probability of extreme events is judged higher now; correlation-aware VaR, used properly, remains a decent risk measure and better than Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Alistair Williams podcast; personal experience with VaR

worldview_premises.premise: In funds whose open trade equity grew to 50-70% of NAV, new investors face a straight 50% drawdown that long-standing investors do not, so sizing on closed equity mainly suits one's own money with an infinite runway.
worldview_premises.support: last year's observation of some managers

decision_process.practice: Track a trend barometer (41 at end of January 2025, neutral) and monthly CTA indices (SG Trend, SG CTA, BTOP50, short-term traders, Bridge flat-fee trend).
decision_process.why: To gauge how trend following is performing; dispersion between indices is notable.

speakers.evidence_style: Anecdote, conferences and podcasts heard (Asness, Williams), index data, and his own experience.

current_views.view: January 2025 was a mixed month for trend: winners in equities after the election, German DAX, coffee, gold and live cattle; zinc was a drag; SG Trend -52bp, SG CTA +20bp, BTOP50 about +70bp, Bridge flat-fee -78bp; MSCI World +3.47%.
A divergent world (central banks acting independently, trade tensions) may favor trend strategies more now.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Rich claims trend following has convexity at no cost, but also says it is exposed to short-term shocks and whipsaws and is not a pure insurance program; the host notes trend skew has reportedly declined. No payoff data are shown.
The claim that few trend followers blow up and no validated 20-30 year records exist for other styles is asserted without evidence or survivorship discussion.
Natural analogies (avalanche, flood, forest fire) support the fragility argument but do not show that low volatility raises tail risk in markets.
'Smooth linear curves later become concave' is shown with LTCM and mean reversion as examples; a counter-case of a smooth strategy that did not fail is not considered.

Rich's definition of the barbell (small linear losses, amplified gains) and the 'unrealised equity could be 5% of the value of the portfolio' remark are not quantified; the open-equity sizing rule is contested by the host.

Rich's own wording says convexity cannot be had from historical statistics yet asserts that trend following has convex payoff; the evidence for the latter is the structure of the rules, not a measured skew.
(reader) The 60/40 critique (no brakes after correlation turned positive) is asserted from the recent correlation shift only; the earlier decades in which bonds did hedge are not discussed.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs the speakers say matter: (1) divergence between central banks (BOJ hiking, ECB cutting, Fed on hold) as a source of dispersion and trends; (2) the stock-bond correlation (positive now) as a break in the basis of 60/40; (3) regime of volatility (long muted periods followed by explosive moves) rather than average volatility; (4) trend persistence, since trend following pays when material trends exist and earns nothing in stagnation; (5) the open-equity share of NAV in trend funds as a risk for new investors. Horizon is the multi-year compounding horizon. Neither speaker forecasts a market direction.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rich's argument is a payoff-shape argument: rather than forecasting, he picks strategy classes (convex) whose payoff survives regime shifts, which is why he dismisses prediction-based risk measures.

(reader) The host's horizon argument and Rich's no-premium claim point to the same unresolved question: how much of trend following's convexity exists at the horizon an investor cares about, given its lag in sudden shocks.
(reader) Both speakers treat dispersion across trend managers as informative about model and market-exposure differences, linking it to the divergent macro environment rather than to randomness.
(reader) The closed-equity discussion implies that risk measured on core capital understates the risk borne by a new investor, which is an allocator-side, not a model-side, problem.
